name: Mewing

angle.text: Users practise mewing in the hope of a more defined jawline, forward midface and better profile, drawing on the orthotropics ideas of John and Mike Mew. The claim that tongue posture reshapes adult facial bone rests on anecdote and before-and-after photos rather than controlled studies.

summary: Resting the whole tongue against the palate to reshape the face; popular online, but no research shows it changes adult jaw structure.
note: The American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence it reshapes the jaw; its originator's son was struck off the UK dental register in 2024.
currentQuick:
Mewing is a do-it-yourself habit of keeping the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, lips closed and teeth lightly together, with nasal breathing. It is named after the British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, who promoted a wider approach called orthotropics. It spread widely on social media from 2019 and became one of the best-known practices in looksmaxxing communities.
Proponents say sustained tongue posture can push the upper jaw forward and sharpen the jawline, with the strongest effects claimed in children. Orthodontic bodies say no credible research shows it reshapes the face. The one controlled study usually cited is a small twin study of orthotropic versus conventional braces treatment, which tested professional orthotropic appliances rather than tongue posture alone.
How it works: The theory holds that the tongue's resting pressure on the palate guides upper-jaw growth forward and outward, and that jaw shape depends heavily on posture and breathing habits rather than genetics alone. Mainstream orthodontics attributes facial form mainly to genetics and growth. Some community members also say the posture temporarily lifts the hyoid bone and tightens the area under the chin, which can change how the jawline looks.
Risks and caveats: Gentle tongue posture is not documented to carry serious risks, though some online posts report masseter enlargement or a worse appearance from forceful versions. The main documented harms concern Mike Mew's clinical practice, which a UK regulatory tribunal examined, rather than the home technique. Orthodontic organizations warn that it may delay evidence-based treatment for real bite or jaw problems.
deepLead:
Mewing is a self-directed practice in which a person rests the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth, keeps the lips sealed and the teeth lightly together, and breathes through the nose, with the stated aim of improving jaw and facial structure . It takes its name from John Mew, a British orthodontist, and his son Mike Mew, who promoted the approach known as orthotropics .
Orthotropics holds that oral posture, especially tongue position, guides facial growth, and that crooked teeth and recessed jaws are largely environmental. Professional orthodontic bodies do not support this, and Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven or pseudoscientific technique . The American Association of Orthodontists has stated there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw .
Interest in mewing rose sharply from January 2019, spreading through social media and looksmaxxing forums . A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery concluded that it is not a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery . Proponents continue to report benefits, particularly for people who began in childhood.

name: Hard mewing

angle.text: Hard mewing is a forceful version of tongue posture that forum users adopt for faster jaw and midface change, sometimes alongside thumb pulling and expanders. Some posters report masseter growth, which would be a muscle effect; the bone-change claim is untested and rests on anecdote.

summary: Mewing with deliberate upward tongue pressure; discussed as a stronger version of tongue posture, with no research testing it and some users reporting masseter growth.
note: No published study has tested it; users report enlarged masseters and tooth gaps in combination with other practices.
currentQuick:
Hard mewing is a looksmaxxing term for pressing the tongue against the palate with deliberate force, as opposed to the light resting posture usually described as mewing. It is discussed on looksmax.org alongside chewing, thumb pulling, chin tucks and palate expansion.
Proponents report forward growth, a wider jaw and better breathing and posture. No published study has examined forceful tongue pressure as an appearance practice, and orthodontic bodies say mewing in general lacks evidence.
How it works: Believers say stronger and more sustained pressure from the tongue on the palate drives more bone remodelling than a relaxed resting posture, extending the orthotropic idea that tongue posture guides upper-jaw growth. Mechanical-loading research shows bone adapts to strain in general, but no study measures what tongue pressure does to the adult facial skeleton.
Risks and caveats: Users on forums report that hard mewing made their masseter muscles wider, changed how their cheeks looked and, in combination with thumb pulling and expanders, opened a gap between the front teeth. These are anecdotal reports. No clinical data exist on forceful tongue pressure.
deepLead:
Hard mewing is a term used in looksmaxxing communities for a more forceful form of mewing, in which a person presses the tongue upward against the palate with deliberate effort rather than simply resting it there . Forum users use it interchangeably with, or as a stage beyond, ordinary mewing, and some threads ask directly how the two differ .
Mewing derives from orthotropics, developed by British orthodontist John Mew, which claims that tongue posture guides facial growth. Professional orthodontic bodies do not support that claim, and the American Association of Orthodontists has stated there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw . No published research addresses hard mewing specifically.

name: Thumb pulling

angle.text: Users pull on the palate with a thumb as a free stand-in for professional palatal expansion, hoping for a wider palate and more forward midface. It is usually paired with mewing and chewing, and the appearance claim rests on forum anecdote rather than studies.

summary: Pulling the palate downward with a thumb to widen the upper jaw; discussed as a free substitute for expanders, with no studies behind it.
note: No clinical study exists; the midpalatal suture generally fuses after puberty, and users report tooth gaps in combined regimens.
currentQuick:
Thumb pulling is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person places a thumb on the roof of the mouth and pulls downward and forward, intending to widen or move the upper jaw. It is presented in forums as a do-it-yourself imitation of the palate expanders used in orthodontics.
Proponents report easier breathing, a feeling of movement in the maxilla and a larger palate. Other forum users call it ineffective, and no published study has tested it.
How it works: The idea is that sustained mechanical force on the palate remodels bone, as in orthodontic expansion. Orthodontic expansion uses fixed appliances that apply controlled force over weeks, and in teenagers and adults the midpalatal suture is generally less open or fused, which is why implant-assisted or surgical expansion is used. Forum users themselves question whether a thumb can produce enough force for long enough.
Risks and caveats: No clinical safety data exist. Orthodontic literature on expansion lists side effects such as a gap between the upper front teeth, pain and bone thinning, but those concern appliances. Forum posts describe diastema after combining thumb pulling with hard mewing and expanders.
deepLead:
Thumb pulling is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which a person pulls on the palate with the thumb, usually downward and forward, in the belief that it can widen the palate or move the maxilla forward . It is discussed as a free alternative to professional palatal expansion and is commonly paired with mewing and chewing.
No published study has tested thumb pulling. Professional palatal expansion, by contrast, is an established orthodontic procedure that uses appliances, usually in children and adolescents, because the midpalatal suture is open early in life and generally fuses after puberty .

name: Chewing for jaw

angle.text: Users chew mastic gum or tough foods to build the masseters and give the lower face a more defined look, often alongside mewing and neck work. Masseter enlargement from chewing is documented in muscle research; changes to jaw bone from chewing are untested.

summary: Chewing tough gum or food to build the masseters and jaw; muscle enlargement is documented, bone change is untested.
note: Heavy chewing is linked in research to jaw muscle fatigue and possible temporomandibular symptoms; one forum user reports worn molars.
currentQuick:
Chewing for jaw, often called jawmaxxing, means chewing tough gum such as mastic or hard foods for long periods to enlarge the masseter muscles and strengthen the jaw. It is popular in looksmaxxing forums as a way to look more defined at the lower face.
Masseter enlargement from heavy chewing is recognised in medical literature. Claims that chewing reshapes the jaw bone or improves the profile have not been studied in published trials.
How it works: The masseter is a main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw, and like other skeletal muscle it can enlarge with sustained use. Proponents add the idea that bone adapts to muscle loading as well. No study tests whether chewing regimens change facial bone in people.
Risks and caveats: Medical sources note that constant gum chewing or clenching can enlarge the masseter and has been linked to temporomandibular problems. A study of 323 adolescent girls examined gum chewing, jaw play and temporomandibular symptoms. A forum user reports worn molars and a face that looked bloated after years of mewing and mastic gum chewing.
deepLead:
Chewing for jaw, also called jawmaxxing, is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which people chew hard gum, particularly mastic gum, or tough foods to develop the jaw muscles and, according to proponents, the jaw's appearance . It is often paired with mewing, chin tucks and neck exercises .
The masseter muscle can enlarge in people who clench or grind their teeth or chew gum constantly, and the enlargement may make the face look asymmetrical or wider . Whether chewing changes the underlying bone, or improves jawline definition, has not been tested in published studies.

name: Facial yoga / face exercises

angle.text: Face exercises are promoted as a natural facelift, with users aiming at firmer cheeks, a sharper jawline and a more lifted look around the eyes and mouth. The sources available include no study measuring appearance outcomes, so the claim rests on practitioner and forum accounts.

summary: Muscle exercises for the face promoted as a natural facelift; the available sources include no study of appearance outcomes.
note: Sources reviewed contain no study measuring appearance change; forum members themselves rank exercises below surgery or appliances.
currentQuick:
Facial yoga and face exercises are routines of deliberate facial-muscle movements, often shown on video, that proponents say tone the cheeks, chin and jaw and soften the signs of ageing. Looksmaxxing communities discuss them as a low-cost option for the cheekbones, chin and jawline.
No clinical study of their effect on appearance is available among the sources used here. Research that exists on facial exercises concerns older adults' mental health, not facial appearance.
How it works: The idea is that strengthening facial muscles lifts and fills the overlying skin, much as exercise builds other muscles. Forum users who discuss the topic add that fat loss and chewing are what change facial shape, and some describe the exercises as a fallback for people who cannot afford surgery.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms appear in the sources used. A forum guide describes the exercises as inferior to surgery, appliances or fillers and as better than nothing for young or low-budget users.
deepLead:
Facial yoga, also called face exercises, is a set of voluntary facial-muscle movements promoted to firm, lift or reshape the face, and is often presented as a natural alternative to cosmetic procedures. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for the cheekbones, nose, chin and jawline .
None of the studies identified for this article tested facial exercises for facial appearance. Small studies of facial exercise programmes in older adults examined mental health and cognition rather than looks .

name: Wolff's law facial loading

angle.text: Wolff's law, a real principle of bone adaptation, is cited in looksmaxxing circles as the theory behind mewing, chewing and pulling practices that aim to reshape the face. Applying it to adult facial bone through tongue posture or chewing is a theory that has not been tested.

summary: The idea that mechanical load remodels facial bone, borrowed from a real principle of bone biology but untested for tongue posture, chewing or pulling.
note: The principle is well supported for bone generally; its application to adult facial reshaping via DIY loading has no published tests.
currentQuick:
Wolff's law is a nineteenth-century principle that bone adapts its structure to the loads placed on it. In looksmaxxing it is the theoretical backbone for mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and bonesmashing: if bone responds to load, the argument goes, loading the face should reshape it.
The general principle, now usually called bone functional adaptation, is well supported by research on bones such as the limbs and spine. Whether the small, specific forces used in facial practices change the adult face has not been tested.
How it works: Bone cells, especially osteocytes, sense mechanical strain and signal bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells. Frost's mechanostat model proposes thresholds of strain at which bone is added, conserved or lost. The faces' bones are described in orthodontic literature as load-bearing, but the loads in daily tongue posture are small and their effect has not been measured.
Risks and caveats: The principle itself carries no risk. Practices justified by it, such as forceful pulling or striking of the face, are discussed separately and are not covered by research support.
deepLead:
Wolff's law states that bone in a healthy animal adapts to the loads placed on it, becoming denser and stronger under greater loading and weaker under less . It is named for the German surgeon and anatomist Julius Wolff (1836-1902), whose 1892 book Das Gesetz der Transformation der Knochen set out the idea . In looksmaxxing communities, 'Wolff's law' is cited as the reason that mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and similar practices are said to reshape the face.
Scientists now generally prefer the term bone functional adaptation: reviewers note that Wolff's original mathematical formulation has been discredited while the broader concept of adaptation to loading is supported by much experimental and observational data . No published study has tested whether tongue posture or other do-it-yourself facial loading remodels the facial skeleton.

name: Orbital rubbing / eye socket massage

angle.text: Users press or rub around the eye socket in the hope of changing orbit shape and giving the eyes a more open, defined look. It is discussed as a non-surgical option for eye-area aesthetics; no study supports bone change from massage, so the claim rests on anecdote.

summary: Pressing or rubbing the eye socket to reshape the eyes; no studies support bone change, and eye rubbing is linked to corneal problems.
note: Eye rubbing is associated with keratoconus in the medical literature.
currentQuick:
Orbital rubbing is a bonehack in which people press or massage the area around the eye socket hoping to change eye shape or the look of the orbit.
No clinical study has tested whether this alters the orbital bones, and community material on it is sparse.
How it works: Believers' idea is that sustained manual pressure remodels bone around the socket. The orbit is a rigid cavity made of seven bones, and no research has examined remodeling by massage.
Risks and caveats: Medical sources associate vigorous eye rubbing with keratoconus progression, and the orbit surrounds the eye and optic structures. Pressure near the eye has not been studied as a cosmetic technique.
deepLead:
Orbital rubbing, also called eye socket massage, is a bonehacking practice in which a person presses or rubs the area around the eye socket in the belief that doing so can change the shape or position of the orbit and therefore the appearance of the eyes. It is discussed as a non-surgical way to alter eye-area aesthetics.
The bony orbit is a cavity formed by seven distinct bones that protects the eye . No published clinical study that the wiki has located has tested whether manual pressure or massage can remodel the adult orbital bones. Separately, medical literature associates vigorous rubbing of the eye itself with progression of the corneal condition keratoconus .

name: Nose bone massaging / nasal bone pushing

angle.text: Users press or massage the nose, usually the bridge, hoping to narrow or reshape it without surgery. It is discussed as a free alternative to rhinoplasty; no study tests it for reshaping, and the medical literature on nasal bones concerns fractures.

summary: Pressing or massaging the nose to narrow it; no study supports reshaping and medical literature covers only fractures.
note: Nasal injury literature shows damage needs professional assessment.
currentQuick:
Nose bone massaging is a bonehack in which people press or massage the nose, usually the bridge, hoping to narrow or reshape it.
No clinical study has tested this on healthy noses; the medical literature on nasal bones is about fractures and surgery.
How it works: Proponents' idea is that repeated pressure moves the nasal bones or the structures around them. Anatomy sources describe a bone-and-cartilage framework that surgeons reshape operatively, and none has examined massage.
Risks and caveats: No studies have measured the effects of self-applied pressure on the nose. Trauma reviews note that injured noses need assessment for septal hematoma, which requires emergency treatment.
deepLead:
Nose bone massaging, or nasal bone pushing, is a bonehacking practice in which a person presses or massages the nose, usually the bridge, in the belief that this can narrow it or change its shape without surgery.
The nasal bones are two small paired bones forming the bridge of the upper third of the nose, joined at the midline and attached to the frontal bone and maxilla . Medical literature on the nasal bones deals almost entirely with fractures and their reduction or surgical correction . No published study that the wiki has located has tested whether pressing or massaging the nose reshapes it in healthy people.

name: Hyoid / neck posture meta

angle.text: Users discuss raising the hyoid and correcting neck posture, together with reducing submental fat, to sharpen the angle between chin and neck. Chin tucks and neck exercises are the usual tools. The sources available address airway anatomy rather than appearance, so the link rests on forum theory.

summary: Raising the hyoid or fixing neck posture for a sharper jawline; no studies address appearance, only airway anatomy.
note: Hyoid position research concerns sleep apnea, not looks; submental injections and surgery carry their own risks.
currentQuick:
The hyoid meta holds that a low hyoid bone or poor neck posture blunts the chin-neck angle and the side profile, and people discuss ways to raise it.
Medical literature on the hyoid is about breathing and swallowing; no study has tested whether exercises move it or change appearance.
How it works: Believers propose that neck posture, exercises or tongue posture shift the hyoid or tighten the area under the chin. Anatomy sources describe the hyoid as muscle-suspended and do not describe an effect on neck contour.
Risks and caveats: No harms are documented for the exercises themselves in the sources reviewed. Related procedures discussed by users, such as submental injections or liposuction, are medical interventions with separate risks.
deepLead:
The hyoid or neck posture meta is a set of beliefs in looksmaxxing communities that the position of the hyoid bone, together with neck posture and submental fat, determines the sharpness of the jawline and neck in profile. Users describe a "low" or "bad" hyoid as flattening the angle between chin and neck, and they discuss ways to "raise" it.
The hyoid is a horseshoe-shaped bone in the front of the neck, between the chin and the thyroid cartilage, held in place by muscles and ligaments rather than by joints with other bones . Medical literature on its position concerns breathing and swallowing rather than appearance: a lower hyoid is associated with obstructive sleep apnea . No published study that the wiki has located has tested whether exercises or posture change the visible neck contour by moving the hyoid in healthy people.

name: Palate expanders (adult)

angle.text: Adults use MARPE or surgically assisted expansion, real orthodontic procedures, with the aim of a wider upper jaw and fuller midface and smile. Expansion is studied for transverse jaw deficiency and breathing; its effect on overall facial appearance is untested.

summary: Adult MARPE or surgical palate expansion for midface width and breathing; real orthodontic procedure, but appearance benefit is untested.
note: Success varies in adults and some need surgical assistance; appearance outcomes are not the focus of trials.
currentQuick:
Palate expanders widen the upper jaw. In adults, miniscrew-assisted (MARPE) or surgically assisted versions are used for a narrow upper jaw, and looksmaxxers discuss them for midface width and breathing.
Trials show skeletal expansion in selected patients, but reviews call efficacy evidence limited and trials rarely measure facial attractiveness.
How it works: A screw-driven appliance is anchored to the teeth, mini-implants in the palate, or both, and turned to separate the midpalatal suture so bone forms in the gap. Adults often need bone anchorage or surgical help because the suture has matured.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include pain, speech changes, a gap between front teeth, tongue sores, periodontal changes and variable success in adults. Treatment is delivered by orthodontists, and surgical versions carry operative risks.
deepLead:
Palate expanders are orthodontic devices that widen the upper jaw (maxilla) so that upper and lower teeth fit together better. They are most often used in children and adolescents, and adult versions, such as miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion, are used for transverse maxillary deficiency in patients whose palatal suture has matured .
In looksmaxxing communities, adult MARPE is discussed as a way to widen the midface, broaden the smile and improve breathing, and some users seek it for aesthetic reasons . Systematic reviews describe the evidence for MARPE in late adolescents and adults as limited, while trials report skeletal expansion and some airway changes in selected patients .

name: Nasal breathing meta

chain: Claimed better jaw and midface development
angle.text: Users favour nasal breathing, sometimes with mouth taping, in the belief it supports jaw and midface structure and a leaner face. Studies in children link mouth breathing to growth changes; whether switching as an adult changes appearance is untested.

summary: Breathing through the nose for better facial development; child studies link mouth breathing to growth changes, adult appearance effects are untested.
note: Mouth taping is little studied and described as risky without supervision.
currentQuick:
The nasal breathing meta says habitual nose breathing supports facial development and airway, and mouth breathing leads to a long narrow face.
Research connects chronic mouth breathing to growth patterns in children, but the link may run both ways and no study tests adult appearance changes.
How it works: Proponents say breathing pattern and tongue posture influence the growing jaw and midface. In medicine, nasal obstruction causes mouth breathing, and treatment focuses on the obstruction.
Risks and caveats: Breathing through the nose is normal physiology. Mouth taping is little researched, and nasal surgery such as turbinate reduction carries surgical risks, with empty nose syndrome raised by some users.
deepLead:
The nasal breathing meta is the looksmaxxing belief that habitually breathing through the nose, rather than the mouth, supports healthy facial development, jaw and midface structure, and appearance. It is closely associated with mewing, mouth taping and discussions of nasal surgery.
Medical literature does describe a relationship between chronic mouth breathing in children and facial growth patterns, sometimes called long face syndrome, though causation can run in either direction . A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of mouth breathing on facial skeletal development in children . Evidence on adults is much thinner, and no study that the wiki has located tests whether adopting nasal breathing in adulthood changes facial appearance.

name: Sleeping position for face symmetry

angle.text: Users sleep on their back in the belief that it avoids pressing one side of the face into a pillow and keeps the face symmetrical. No study links sleep posture to facial symmetry, so the idea rests on forum anecdote.

summary: Sleeping on your back to keep the face symmetrical; no study links sleep posture to facial symmetry.
note: Back sleeping can worsen positional sleep apnea in some people.
currentQuick:
The belief is that sleeping on one side presses and distorts the face over years, so sleeping on the back protects symmetry.
No study has tested this. General references on symmetry list development, aging and prenatal factors as causes of asymmetry, and sleep position only appears as one contributor to wrinkles.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is prolonged mechanical pressure on one side of the face during sleep. This has not been measured in published research.
Risks and caveats: Sleep-position reviews note that back sleeping can worsen positional sleep apnea and snoring in some people. No documented harms are specific to this claim.
deepLead:
Sleeping position for face symmetry is a looksmaxxing belief that the posture a person sleeps in affects facial symmetry, with sleeping on the back often described as the way to avoid asymmetry caused by pressing one side of the face into a pillow.
Mainstream sources do not establish that sleep posture determines facial symmetry. A general reference on facial symmetry lists development, aging and prenatal factors among causes of asymmetry and does not mention sleep posture . A general reference on skin wrinkles lists habitual sleeping positions as one of several contributors to wrinkles, without describing the size of the effect .

name: Cortisol face / stress face claims

angle.text: Forum posters attribute a rounded, puffy or tired-looking face to stress and high cortisol, and aim to lower stress for a leaner look. Facial rounding is documented in medicine with sustained hormone excess; everyday stress has not been tested for this effect.

summary: The idea that stress hormones puff up and age your face; the medical 'moon face' is real but tied to sustained hormone excess, and nothing tests everyday stress.
note: Facial rounding of the kind described in medicine is linked to prolonged glucocorticoid excess (Cushing's syndrome or steroid medication), which needs clinical assessment.
currentQuick:
'Cortisol face' is an informal term for a puffy, rounded or tired-looking face that some people attribute to stress and elevated cortisol, the body's main stress-response hormone. It circulates in wellness and appearance discussions, and looksmaxxing forums also use 'cortisol spikes' as shorthand for stress and anxiety reactions.
In medicine, a rounded face ('moon face') is a recognised sign of Cushing's syndrome, which results from prolonged exposure to excess glucocorticoids, most often from prescribed steroid drugs. Clinical sources describe it as arising from rare hormonal disorders, not from ordinary day-to-day stress, and no published study in this area has measured facial appearance against everyday stress.
How it works: Cortisol raises blood sugar, mobilises energy, suppresses inflammation and acts on receptors that increase sodium and water retention. When glucocorticoid exposure is sustained at high levels, clinicians describe fat redistribution to the trunk and face, thinner skin, easy bruising and facial redness. Believers extend this to chronic stress, proposing that repeated cortisol surges puff and age the face; that extension has not been tested directly.
Risks and caveats: Because the term is a popular claim rather than a practice, the main risk discussed is misattribution: facial swelling, redness or rounding can have many causes, and Cushing's syndrome is a medical condition that clinicians diagnose with testing. Some herbal supplements have been reported to contain undisclosed glucocorticoids, and steroid medicines themselves can produce these facial changes.
deepLead:
'Cortisol face' or 'stress face' is an informal term for a rounded, puffy or aged-looking face that some people attribute to stress and elevated levels of the hormone cortisol. Cortisol is the main glucocorticoid released in response to stress and low blood sugar; it raises blood glucose, mobilises energy stores, suppresses inflammation and increases sodium and water retention.
The medical concept behind the term is 'moon face', a rounded and often reddened face described as a sign of Cushing's syndrome, the condition caused by prolonged exposure to excess glucocorticoids. The most common cause is glucocorticoid medication such as prednisone; others include pituitary or adrenal tumours and ACTH-producing tumours elsewhere in the body. Reference sources state that the 'cortisol face' look arises from these rare hormonal disorders rather than from everyday stress.
No published human study identified for this article has tested whether ordinary psychological stress or transient cortisol spikes change facial appearance. Reviews of cortisol describe short-term spikes as adaptive, with health problems linked to sustained or abnormal levels. In looksmaxxing communities, 'cortisol spikes' is more often used as slang for anxiety or stress reactions than as a claim about the face.

name: Limb lengthening surgery (LL)

angle.text: Users pursue limb lengthening to add permanent height, since cutting and slowly extending the femurs or tibias increases leg length, a measurable change. The technique is established in medicine for limb discrepancy and deformity and is also performed electively for cosmetic height gain.

summary: Cutting and gradually extending the femurs or tibias to add height; the only route to permanent added stature, but it is major surgery with months of recovery and documented complications.
note: Major orthopaedic surgery: reported complications include infection, nonunion, nerve injury, joint stiffness and additional operations.
currentQuick:
Limb lengthening is an orthopaedic procedure in which a leg bone is cut and then slowly pulled apart so that new bone forms in the gap. It was developed to treat limb-length differences, deformities and dwarfism conditions such as achondroplasia, and it is also performed electively for people who want to be taller. In looksmaxxing forums it is the best-known height surgery, discussed by people who feel height limits their appearance or dating prospects.
The technique has decades of clinical literature behind it, mostly in medical (non-cosmetic) patients. Gains of several centimetres are described in clinical series, and the new bone is permanent. Forum users stress cost, months of rehabilitation and the possibility of complications, and some weigh it against other surgeries or purchases.
How it works: After the bone is cut, a week or so is allowed for early healing and the two segments are then separated at roughly a millimetre a day, split into several small steps. Soft tissue and bone regenerate in the gap, a process called distraction osteogenesis described by Gavriil Ilizarov. The bone then consolidates over further weeks or months. Devices include external frames and fixators, internal nails that are lengthened mechanically or magnetically, and combinations of the two.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include pin-site and deep infection, bone that fails to heal, deformity, hardware failure, joint contractures, nerve injury and further operations. A classic Ilizarov-era paper grouped difficulties into problems, obstacles and true complications. China's health ministry banned the procedure in 2006 after serious side effects, according to one encyclopedia summary, and cosmetic limb lengthening in India has been described as high-demand and largely unregulated. Cos
deepLead:
Limb lengthening, often abbreviated 'LL' in looksmaxxing communities, is a surgical method that increases the length of a limb bone by cutting it and slowly separating the two ends while new bone and soft tissue form between them. This biological process is called distraction osteogenesis. It is used in medicine for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction, bone defects and skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia, and is also performed electively for cosmetic height gain.
The modern method grew out of work by Soviet surgeon Gavriil Ilizarov, whose circular external fixator and slow-distraction protocols made bone lengthening reliable enough for widespread use, building on earlier attempts such as Alessandro Codivilla's 1905 series, which had high rates of infection and failed healing. Later techniques use internal lengthening nails, including mechanically or magnetically driven ones, in place of or alongside external frames.
Published research is substantial for medical indications but thinner for purely cosmetic lengthening in otherwise healthy people. Clinical papers report a range of complications, and the literature on complications distinguishes minor problems resolved without surgery from obstacles requiring operations and true complications. On forums such as looksmax.org, LL is often described as the only way to add stature beyond genetic potential, and the discussion centres on cost, countries and surgeons, recovery and whether the gain is worthwhile.

name: Cosmetic leg lengthening (Precice nails)

angle.text: The Precice nail is a magnetically lengthened internal implant that lets people gain height without an external frame, and the added stature is measurable. It is well studied for medical limb lengthening, with limited data specific to cosmetic use.

summary: Height surgery using a magnetically lengthened nail inside the bone instead of an external frame; well studied for medical lengthening, with limited cosmetic-specific data.
note: Major surgery: complications reported include nail bending, nonunion and other problems; the Precice nail is a medical device approved for limb-length discrepancy, not a cosmetic product.
currentQuick:
The Precice nail is an implant placed inside the long bone after the bone is cut. A magnet held outside the leg remotely drives the nail to lengthen in small daily steps, so the bone gradually grows longer without an external frame. It was developed for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction and bone defects, and it has also been adopted for cosmetic stature lengthening, where healthy adults seek extra height.
The published literature on Precice is mostly case series and reviews in medical patients, in both adults and children. A 2025 meta-analysis and a scoping review have begun to examine cosmetic lengthening specifically, including complications and the quality-of-life measures used.
How it works: After the femur or tibia is cut, a telescoping intramedullary nail is fixed inside the canal. An external remote control with a magnet makes the nail lengthen by a small controlled amount per day, producing new bone through distraction osteogenesis. Orthopaedic papers evaluating the device report the distraction is accurate and the bone heals well, with the nail also able to shorten when needed.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include nail bending or deformation under load, failure of the bone to heal, joint stiffness and other complications; some failures have been attributed to excessive loading of the limb. Surgeons describe the procedure as demanding, with weeks to months of limited weight-bearing and rehabilitation. Cosmetic use is elective and falls outside the device's usual medical indications.
deepLead:
The Precice nail is a motorless, magnetically driven intramedullary (inside-the-bone) lengthening nail made by Ellipse Technologies, later NuVasive. An external remote control uses a magnet to lengthen the implant in small controlled increments after the bone has been cut, so the bone grows longer through distraction osteogenesis without an external fixator. A 2014 study of the device noted that earlier internal lengthening designs had imprecise distraction, with nerve injuries, joint contractures and nonunion, and that the magnet-operated Precice nail had recently been cleared by the FDA.
The nail is used for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction, humeral lengthening and bone transport after tumour resection, and is also used in cosmetic stature lengthening. Expert commentary describes strong bone healing with the retrograde femoral nail, and attributes the few failures to excessive loading of the limb and implant.
Cosmetic lengthening is a smaller part of the literature. A 2025 meta-analysis compared external fixation with intramedullary nailing for cosmetic lengthening in terms of complications and functional outcomes, and a 2025 scoping review found that existing studies capture clinical results better than patient-centred life-impact outcomes.

name: HGH for height

angle.text: People discuss growth hormone to gain height, either as teenagers or past puberty. It is studied in children with short stature, with modest gains; use in healthy adults with closed growth plates for height is untested.

summary: Using growth hormone to try to grow taller; studied in children with short stature, with modest gains, and untested for healthy adults with closed growth plates.
note: Prescription-only; trials are in children with growth plates open. Evidence for height gain in healthy adults is not available, and long-term risks in healthy adults are described as unknown.
currentQuick:
Human growth hormone (HGH, somatropin) is a prescription injectable used medically for growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, small-for-gestational-age short stature and several other conditions. 'HGH for height' refers to using it, medically or non-medically, to increase height in someone who is short for reasons other than a hormone deficiency, or to try for extra height in the looksmaxxing context.
In clinical trials of children with idiopathic short stature, treatment over several years has been reported to add a few centimetres of adult height on average. Paediatric endocrinology papers debate whether this is meaningful, call it 'cosmetic endocrinology' and discuss cost and ethics. On forums, some users who are past their teenage years ask whether HGH can still add height; no clinical trial identified for this article tests that.
How it works: Growth hormone acts on the liver and tissues to raise IGF-1 and stimulates growth at the growth plates in the long bones of children and adolescents. Height gain requires open growth plates; after the plates fuse, bones cannot lengthen from growth stimulation. Forum users also talk about growth-hormone-releasing peptides and IGF-1 analogues as alternatives, which are separate and largely unstudied for this purpose.
Risks and caveats: Documented effects of growth hormone therapy include reduced insulin sensitivity, and some cancer-subgroup signals in large studies. A 2003 editorial cautioned against off-label use and noted that long-term risks in healthy adults are unknown. Forum users report changes such as a widening nose, and cost can be very high. Growth hormone is a prescription drug in most countries, and counterfeit or mislabelled products have been reported in the gray market.
deepLead:
Human growth hormone (HGH), also called somatropin, is a peptide hormone produced by the pituitary gland and available as a recombinant prescription drug. 'HGH for height' refers to using it to increase stature, either in children who are short without a hormone deficiency (so-called idiopathic short stature) or, in looksmaxxing communities, by people who hope to gain height beyond what they would reach naturally.
Approved uses described in medical references include growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney failure, Prader-Willi syndrome, intrauterine growth retardation and short-stature homeobox gene deficiency; the FDA approved Humatrope for idiopathic short stature in 2003. Trials in extreme idiopathic short stature reported about 4 to 8 cm of added adult height after roughly four years of treatment, and in Turner syndrome a median gain of about 5 to 8 cm, with gains that appear dose-dependent.
The paediatric literature calls extending growth-hormone treatment to children without deficiency 'cosmetic endocrinology' and recommends restraint, informed assent and cost-conscious practice. No clinical trial identified for this article has tested growth hormone for height in healthy adults whose growth plates have closed; a 2003 journal editorial cautioned that long-term risks in healthy adults are unknown.

name: Letrozole / aromatase inhibitors for height

angle.text: Teenagers and parents discuss aromatase inhibitors as a way to slow bone maturation and extend growth for extra height. They have been trialled in boys with short stature; their use for height in healthy people is off-label and has no published evidence.

summary: Using aromatase inhibitors to slow bone maturation and extend growth; trialled in boys with short stature, with no published evidence for healthy adults.
note: Prescription drugs approved for other uses (such as breast cancer); height use is off-label and studied only in boys with open growth plates.
currentQuick:
Aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole block the enzyme that converts androgens into oestrogen. Because oestrogen drives the closing of growth plates in both sexes, researchers have tested these drugs in adolescent boys with short stature or delayed puberty, hoping to slow bone maturation and give more time to grow.
The idea circulates in height-focused communities as a way to 'delay growth plate closure'. Published research relevant to it is limited to paediatric studies, including a registered phase 3 trial of aromatase inhibitors alone and with growth hormone in adolescent boys with idiopathic short stature. No study identified for this article tests the approach in healthy adults.
How it works: Aromatase inhibitors reduce oestrogen production. Lower oestrogen slows growth-plate fusion, which in theory leaves a longer window for growth. Letrozole is a nonsteroidal, reversible inhibitor; other agents include anastrozole and the steroidal exemestane. A meta-analysis cited in encyclopedia sources found letrozole safe and effective for improving height and puberty outcomes in children with constitutional delay of growth and puberty.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources list aromatase inhibitors as causing hot flushes, joint pain and fatigue, with concern for bone density loss and raised cholesterol with long use, and note they are contraindicated in pregnancy and in premenopausal women for their approved indication. They are prescription-only in the US, UK and EU. Sources note slowed bone maturation can be an effect in children; effects of use for height in healthy people are unstudied.
deepLead:
Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are drugs that block aromatase, the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone into oestrogens. Letrozole and anastrozole are reversible nonsteroidal inhibitors, and exemestane is an irreversible steroidal one. They are approved mainly for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
'AI for height' refers to the off-label idea of using these drugs to lower oestrogen in adolescents, slowing growth-plate closure and extending the growing period. Reference sources describe AIs being used experimentally in boys with delayed puberty and idiopathic short stature, where reduced oestrogen slows growth-plate fusion and gives growth hormone more time to work. A meta-analysis of seven randomised trials, summarised in an encyclopedia entry, found letrozole safe and effective for improving height and puberty outcomes in children with constitutional delay of growth and puberty.
A registered phase 3 trial tested aromatase inhibitors alone and combined with growth hormone in 76 adolescent boys with idiopathic short stature. No study identified for this article has tested AIs for height in healthy adults with closed growth plates, and no forum material was identified for this entry.

name: Hanging / stretching for height

angle.text: Users hang from bars and stretch to decompress the spine and recover or hold height. Brief increases in spinal length are reported after decompression; a lasting gain in adult height has not been tested.

summary: Hanging and stretching to decompress the spine for height; any gain reported is brief, and no trial tests lasting growth in adults.
note: Reference sources describe only short-term spinal elongation; adult height is largely genetic.
currentQuick:
Hanging or stretching for height means using bar hangs, traction or stretch routines to decompress the spine in the hope of gaining height. It circulates in height-focused looksmaxxing spaces.
Reference sources describe daily height variation of around 1 to 1.5 cm and short-lived elongation after traction, but report no strong evidence of lasting gains in healthy adults.
How it works: The idea is that gravity compresses the discs through the day and sustained traction restores or lengthens the spine. Measured effects in related research are short-term and largely reverse within about an hour.
Risks and caveats: Plain hanging is not specifically covered in the sources reviewed. Related inversion devices carry documented cautions for people with heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma or pregnancy.
deepLead:
Hanging or stretching for height is a practice in height-focused looksmaxxing communities in which people hang from a bar, use traction or stretching routines, or otherwise aim to decompress the spine in the hope of gaining or recovering height. It is also discussed under the terms decompression and spinal decompression. The underlying idea is that gravity compresses the intervertebral discs over the day and that sustained traction can restore or add length to the spine.
Reference sources describe daily height variation: in one study cited by Wikipedia, 100 children lost an average of about 1.5 cm between morning and late afternoon. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, reports that radiographic studies of inversion and traction show temporary spinal elongation that largely reverses within about an hour, and that no strong evidence exists for lasting multi-centimetre height gains in healthy adults. Wikipedia notes that non-surgical spinal decompression has been studied mainly as a treatment for back pain, with a review finding very limited evidence for its effectiveness.
Wikipedia reports that height is largely determined by genetics (60 to 80 percent heritability in twin studies) and by childhood nutrition and health. No published trial found for this article has tested hanging or stretching routines as a way to increase adult height.

name: Height-increasing supplements

angle.text: Teenagers and adults ask about vitamin, mineral and herbal blends sold to help them grow taller or reach their genetic potential. Adequate nutrition supports normal growth in childhood; no trial backs these products for adding height in adults.

summary: OTC pills sold to make you taller; height is mostly genetic and no trial backs them for adults.
note: No published trials of marketed height supplements were found.
currentQuick:
Height supplements are over-the-counter blends marketed to help people grow taller. Forum users ask whether they help teens or adults, and some call them costly and slow.
Reference sources describe height as mostly genetic and shaped by childhood nutrition. No trial of a marketed height supplement was found.
How it works: Marketers say the vitamins and minerals support the nutrients growth needs. Sources describe nutrition as affecting growth in childhood, but none tests these products.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to height supplements were located. Prescription growth hormone is a separate, medically supervised treatment.
deepLead:
Height-increasing supplements are over-the-counter products, typically vitamin, mineral, amino-acid or herbal blends, marketed with the claim that they help people grow taller or reach their genetic height potential. They are discussed in height-focused looksmaxxing communities, where users ask whether growth pills work for teenagers or adults.
Reference sources describe height as strongly heritable (60 to 80 percent in twin studies) and influenced by childhood nutrition and health, and report that chronic malnutrition can stunt growth. The medical treatment for short stature described in reference sources is prescription growth hormone, which is given under specialist care. No published trial of a marketed height supplement in healthy people was located for this article.

name: Squatmaxxing / spinal loading

angle.text: Users squat heavily to build legs and improve physique proportions, and some wonder whether it changes how tall they look. Leg development from squatting is well established as muscle growth; no source ties squatting to a gain in height.

summary: Squat-focused leg training; discussed for physique proportions, with no source tying it to height.
note: Wikipedia notes torso over-flexion raises lower-back forces; no height effect is documented.
currentQuick:
Squatmaxxing means training squats to build the legs and improve physique proportions. A looksmax.org thread discusses whether it suits wide-waisted people.
Sources describe the squat's muscles and injury considerations but do not link it to height.
How it works: The squat loads the legs and glutes while the spinal muscles and abdominals stabilise the trunk, which also compresses the spine under weight.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes that poor form, especially over-flexing the torso, raises lower-back forces and can risk disc herniation.
deepLead:
Squatmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for building the legs and lower body through squats, either to improve physique proportions or, in some discussions, to affect how tall or strong a person looks. A looksmax.org thread titled Squatmaxxing asks whether leg development suits people with a wide waist, and a reply asks the original poster about body fat percentage, gym training and height.
The sources reviewed describe the squat as a compound exercise working the quadriceps, glutes, adductors and calves, with the spinal erectors and abdominals acting as stabilisers. They do not describe any effect of squatting on height. The related idea of spinal loading, meaning compression of the spine under weight, is addressed in height literature mainly through daily height variation.
